description_full: The J. M. Smucker Company manufactures and markets branded food and beverage products worldwide. The company operates through five segments: U.S. Retail Coffee, U.S. Retail Frozen Handheld and Spreads, U.S. Retail Pet Foods, Sweet Baked Snacks, and Away From Home. It offers coffee, sweet baked goods, pet snacks, frozen handheld products, peanut butter, cat and dog food, fruit and specialty spreads, cookies, frozen sandwiches and snacks, hot beverages, portion control products, toppings and syrups, baking mixes and ingredients, and flour. The company provides its products under the Folgers, Café Bustelo, Dunkin', Jif, Smucker's, Uncrustables, Meow Mix, Milk-Bone, Pup-Peroni, Canine Carry Outs, Hostess, and 1850 brand names. It sells its products through direct sales and brokers to food retailers, club stores, discount and dollar stores, online retailers, pet specialty stores, distributors, drug stores, military commissaries, mass merchandisers, supermarket chains, national mass retailers, convenience stores, vending channels, and foodservice distributors and operators. The J. M. Smucker Company was founded in 1897 and is headquartered in Orrville, Ohio.

financial_summary: The J.M. Smucker Company is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $13.6B market cap on $9.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 3% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 37%.
The business throws off $1.2B in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 9.9× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 9.6×.

Shareholder yield of 3.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 2.3% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 4% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.50x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.3% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-24.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 26% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 7% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 0.28, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $147.2M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 19% in the 2020 crash, 16% in the 2022 bear market and 33% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $104 (margin of safety -22%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 35%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $18.54 to $353 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Consumer Defensive peers: cheaper on P/FCF 11.7 vs 15.1, richer on P/E 59.3 vs 18.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 328% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 8.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 16 covering analysts target $144 on average, 13% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 6.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.60).
It runs a 37% gross margin and converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
It spends 0.8% of revenue on R&D and 0.3% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 9.9x net debt to EBITDA ($44.1M of cash against $7.0B of debt), with interest covered 9.6x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.34 in the distress zone.
The current ratio of 0.78 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.0% over 3 years, 2.5% over 5 years and 1.5% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -1.7% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 3.5% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 15, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 20.3% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.3%, and institutions hold 90%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $5.8M sold).
It returns 3.5% a year to shareholders (0.0% in buybacks and 3.5% in dividends).
It pays out 201% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: CEO pay is $3.8M, and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
